Seven stages
1. Brief
2. Expert input
3. Outline (AI-assisted)
4. Draft from notes (markers)
5. Human edit
6. Fact-check + expert review
7. Publish + monitor
scenes.visual: A seven-station timeline; each station lights up with an icon and a small gate symbol showing its quality check.

scenes.narration: Now the drafting prompt, which does most of the work of keeping things honest. It says: use only the brief and expert notes. Don't add statistics, prices, dates, laws or claims that aren't in the notes. Where a fact is needed but missing, write MISSING and what's needed. Where a claim must be checked, append VERIFY. Follow the outline, start each section with a one or two sentence answer, and don't invent case studies or quotes. Those markers turn hidden risks into visible to do items.
scenes.onScreen:
The drafting prompt
• Only brief + expert notes
• No new stats, prices, dates, laws
• [MISSING: …] for gaps
• [VERIFY] for claims
• No invented cases or quotes
scenes.visual: Code walkthrough: the drafting prompt appears on a dark panel; each rule highlights; a sample draft then shows a highlighted [MISSING: current fee] marker.

scenes.narration: After a human edit, you can run a second prompt as an extra pair of eyes. It lists claims without a cited source, sentences so generic they could appear on any site, sections that don't answer their heading, and places where first hand experience from the notes could be used but isn't. It quotes exact sentences and doesn't rewrite anything. Important: this helps editors, but it is not fact checking. A person still checks every claim against a source.
scenes.onScreen:
The review prompt
• Unsourced claims
• Generic sentences
• Sections not answering headings
• Unused experience
(Helps editors; not fact-checking)
scenes.visual: A draft with four types of highlights appearing in different colours; a sidebar lists quoted sentences under four headings.

scenes.narration: Worked example one, simple. A solo travel blogger uses AI to turn her voice notes from a trip to Hunza into a structured guide. The draft contains a MISSING marker for current jeep hire prices, and a VERIFY marker on road conditions in spring. She calls the guesthouse to confirm prices, checks recent official updates on the road, adds her own photos, and rewrites the intro in her voice. The AI saved her hours of structuring. She supplied everything that makes it worth reading.

• [VERIFY] roads → official updates

Each guide starts with a thirty minute recorded interview with an engineer. The transcript and brief feed the AI assisted outline and draft. An editor handles voice and examples, and the engineer signs off. The pre publish script catches two drafts with unresolved VERIFY markers on API limits, which turn out to be outdated in the transcript. Output quadruples, and each guide still has specifics only their engineers could provide.

scenes.narration: That pre publish script is simple. It reads a draft and blocks it if there are unresolved MISSING, VERIFY or to do markers, if there's no reviewed by line, or if there are fewer than two cited sources. Adapt the rules to your house style, for example requiring an author line and a last reviewed date for money or health topics. Then add governance: a one page AI content policy covering approved tools, what must never be pasted into them, where AI assistance is disclosed, who signs off YMYL content, and how often the policy is reviewed.
scenes.onScreen:
Checks + governance
• Script blocks: markers, no reviewer, <2 sources
• One-page AI policy: tools, data, disclosure, sign-off, review cycle
scenes.visual: Code walkthrough of the checker script; then a one-page policy document with five headings slides in.

scenes.narration: Let's pause on what the editor actually does, because it's more than fixing typos. First, voice: does this sound like us, or like every other site? Second, specificity: are the examples real and from our notes, or generic? Third, structure: does every section answer its heading, answer first? Fourth, cuts: what can go without losing anything? AI drafts often pad. Fifth, risk: any claims that need a source, any YMYL advice that needs expert review? A good editor often removes a fifth of an AI draft and makes the rest sharper.
scenes.onScreen:
The editor's five passes
• Voice
• Specificity
• Structure
• Cuts (remove padding)
• Risk (sources, YMYL)
scenes.visual: An AI draft document gets five coloured editing passes; a word counter drops by about a fifth; highlighted generic phrases are replaced with specific examples.

scenes.narration: And scale with care. AI makes it tempting to publish hundreds of pages. Google's scaled content abuse policy targets pages generated primarily to manipulate rankings, however they're produced. Keep volume tied to your capacity for expert input and editorial review. If editors are spending two minutes per draft, the review has become a rubber stamp, and you're publishing too much. Also keep an eye on evolving rules on AI transparency in your markets, like the EU AI Act.
scenes.onScreen:
Scale with care
• Volume ≤ review capacity
• 2-minute reviews = rubber stamp
• Watch AI transparency rules
scenes.visual: A capacity gauge labelled 'editorial review' with a volume needle; when the needle passes the red line, a rubber-stamp icon appears with a warning.

lessons.title: Content decay and the refresh playbook
lessons.body:
### What content decay is

**Content decay** is the gradual decline in a page's search performance after it peaks. It is normal: facts date, competitors publish better pages, intent shifts, SERP features (including AI Overviews) change how many people click, and the page itself accumulates broken links or outdated screenshots. On many established sites, refreshing existing pages is one of the highest-return activities available — the page already has history, links and relevance.

### Diagnose before you refresh

Decay has different causes, and each needs a different fix:

| Pattern in Search Console | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Impressions stable, clicks and CTR down, position stable | SERP change — more features or AI answers satisfying the query | Improve title/snippet appeal; add depth, tools or first-hand elements that earn the click; consider targeting related sub-questions |
| Impressions and position down | Competitors improved, or content outdated | Refresh substance: current facts, better structure, original elements |
| Impressions down, position stable | Demand fell (seasonality, trend) | Check Google Trends; maybe nothing to fix |
| Queries shifted to a different intent | Intent change | Rework the page or create a better-matched page |
| Sudden drop across many pages | Technical issue or site-wide change | Check indexing, robots, canonicals, redirects; algorithm update timing |

Always compare **like-for-like periods** (for example the last 3 months vs the same 3 months last year) to avoid mistaking seasonality for decay.

### The refresh playbook

1. **Re-read the SERP.** What ranks now? Has the dominant type or format changed? What would still earn a click?
2. **Update facts.** Prices, laws, dates, product details, screenshots — verified against sources.
3. **Add what others lack.** New first-hand examples, data, photos, a calculator or checklist, an expert quote.
4. **Improve structure.** Answer-first summaries, clearer headings, tables where they help.
5. **Tighten.** Remove outdated or padded sections. Longer is not better.
6. **Refresh internal links** — to newer pages, and from newer pages back to this one.
7. **Update on-page elements** — title and meta description if they no longer reflect the content.
8. **Update `dateModified` honestly.** Google advises against changing dates to appear fresh without substantial changes; show a "last updated" date only when the content materially changed.
9. **Request indexing** for important pages via URL Inspection, and annotate the change date.

### Hands-on: find decaying pages with Python

Using two Search Console exports (Pages tab) for comparable periods, or the API:

```python
import pandas as pd

prev = pd.read_csv("pages_2025-06_to_2025-08.csv").rename(columns=str.lower)   # columns: page, clicks, impressions, position
curr = pd.read_csv("pages_2026-06_to_2026-08.csv").rename(columns=str.lower)
df = prev.merge(curr, on="page", how="outer", suffixes=("_prev", "_curr")).fillna(0)
df["click_change"] = df["clicks_curr"] - df["clicks_prev"]
df["click_change_pct"] = df["click_change"] / df["clicks_prev"].where(df["clicks_prev"] > 0)
df["pattern"] = "other"
df.loc[(df["impressions_curr"] >= 0.9 * df["impressions_prev"]) & (df["click_change_pct"] <= -0.25), "pattern"] = "CTR drop (SERP change?)"
df.loc[(df["impressions_curr"] < 0.75 * df["impressions_prev"]) & (df["position_curr"] > df["position_prev"] + 2), "pattern"] = "ranking loss"
decaying = df[(df["clicks_prev"] >= 50) & (df["click_change_pct"] <= -0.25)]
print(decaying.sort_values("click_change").head(25)[["page", "clicks_prev", "clicks_curr", "pattern"]])
decaying.to_csv("refresh_candidates.csv", index=False)
```

(Thresholds are illustrative. Note that position values from exports are averages; treat the pattern labels as prompts to investigate, not diagnoses.)

### Refreshing for AI answers without chasing gimmicks

When a query now shows an AI Overview, the refresh question is "what does our page offer that a summary can't?" Useful answers include a downloadable checklist or calendar, a calculator, current local prices, original photos, a worked example with real numbers, or a named expert's judgement on trade-offs. Google's May 2026 guidance says you don't need to rewrite pages into "AI-friendly" fragments; a clear answer-first structure plus genuinely original elements serves both readers and AI features.

### Measure the refresh

Record the refresh date in an annotation log, then compare the 28 days after re-indexing with the 28 days before *and* with the same period last year. Watch impressions, clicks, CTR and the mix of queries (new sub-questions appearing is a good sign), plus conversions in GA4. Give it 4–8 weeks before judging, and resist refreshing the same page again before then.

### A refresh calendar

Tier pages: **Tier 1** (revenue or high-traffic pages) reviewed quarterly; **Tier 2** twice a year; **Tier 3** annually or when a trigger fires (law change, price change, product update). Seasonal pages get refreshed 6–8 weeks before their peak.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A UK tax-advice blog's "self-assessment deadlines" guide loses a third of its clicks year-on-year while impressions stay flat and position is unchanged. The SERP now shows an AI Overview answering the basic deadline question. The team refreshes the guide around what still earns a click: a downloadable deadline calendar, worked examples for first-time filers, a penalties calculator explained step by step, and a named chartered accountant's tips — with every date checked against GOV.UK. They rewrite the title to promise the calendar and examples. Clicks recover partially, and time on page and enquiries rise.

### Common mistakes

- Refreshing by changing the date and a few words.
- Treating seasonality as decay.
- Rewriting a page that still performs because it's "old".
- Forgetting internal links from newer pages.
keyTakeaways: Content decay is normal; diagnose the cause (SERP change, competitors, demand, intent, technical) before acting.
Compare like-for-like periods to separate decay from seasonality.
A real refresh updates facts, adds original elements, improves structure, tightens and refreshes internal links.
Only update dates when content materially changes; tier pages into a refresh calendar.

lessons.title: Content pruning and consolidation without losing value
lessons.body:
### What pruning is — and isn't

**Content pruning** means deciding, page by page, whether low-performing content should be improved, merged into a stronger page, kept as is, taken out of the index, or removed. The goal is a site where every indexable page is useful to someone. It is **not** a trick: Google has said that deleting content simply because it's old isn't a ranking strategy, and pages that are useful to a small audience (a niche FAQ, a policy page, an archive people cite) can be worth keeping even with little search traffic.

Why prune at all? Because large volumes of thin, outdated or overlapping pages confuse readers, split relevance between near-duplicates (cannibalisation), waste crawling on large sites, and — since helpful content signals are part of core ranking — can weigh on how the site as a whole is perceived.

### The five options

| Option | When | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep** | Useful to users even with low search traffic (policies, niche answers, cited archives) | Leave; maybe improve internal linking |
| **Improve** | Topic matters, page is weak or outdated | Refresh playbook (previous lesson) |
| **Consolidate (merge + 301)** | Several pages cover the same intent; one should own it | Merge the best content into the strongest URL; 301-redirect the others to it; update internal links |
| **Noindex** | Page is useful for users on site but not as a search landing page (thin tag pages, internal search results, some filter pages) | `noindex` meta tag; keep crawlable so the tag is seen |
| **Remove (404/410)** | No value to users, no meaningful links or traffic, no equivalent to redirect to | Return 404/410; remove internal links and sitemap entries |

Redirect only to a **genuinely equivalent** page. Redirecting everything to the home page is treated like a soft 404 and wastes whatever value the old page had.

### Hands-on: a pruning decision sheet

Gather per URL: Search Console clicks and impressions (12 months), GA4 engaged sessions and conversions, referring domains from your backlink tool, word count and last updated date (from a crawl), and the primary query/intent. Then:

```text
A URL | B Clicks 12m | C Impressions 12m | D Conversions | E Ref. domains | F Intent group | G Same intent as (URL)
H Suggested action:
=IF(OR(D2>0, B2>=100), "keep/improve",
  IF(G2<>"", "consolidate into "&G2,
  IF(E2>=3, "improve or redirect to closest equivalent",
  IF(C2>=500, "improve (demand exists)", "review: noindex or remove"))))
```

The formula only *suggests*; a person decides, especially for pages with legal, compliance or brand importance. Thresholds are illustrative — scale them to your site.

### Find overlapping pages (cannibalisation candidates) in Python

```python
import pandas as pd

rows = pd.read_csv("gsc_query_page_12m.csv")          # columns: query, page, clicks, impressions
rows = rows[rows["impressions"] >= 50]
per_query = rows.groupby("query").agg(pages=("page", "nunique"), impressions=("impressions", "sum"))
multi = per_query[per_query["pages"] >= 2].sort_values("impressions", ascending=False)
detail = rows[rows["query"].isin(multi.index)].sort_values(["query", "clicks"], ascending=[True, False])
print(detail.head(40))
detail.to_csv("cannibalisation_candidates.csv", index=False)
```

Two URLs sharing a query isn't automatically a problem (a guide and a product page can both be right). Look for pairs with the **same intent** that swap positions.

### Consolidation checklist

1. Pick the target URL (usually the one with the most links, traffic or best fit).
2. Merge the unique, still-accurate content from the others into it; refresh the whole page.
3. 301-redirect each merged URL to the target (avoid chains).
4. Update internal links to point directly to the target.
5. Remove merged URLs from the XML sitemap.
6. Annotate the date; watch the target's impressions and queries over the next 4–8 weeks.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A Dubai real-estate blog has 14 separate posts on "Dubai Golden Visa" written over three years, with conflicting and outdated information. The team keeps one comprehensive, expert-reviewed guide (verified against official sources, with a "last reviewed" date), merges the still-useful sections from six others, 301-redirects them, noindexes two news-style posts that are historically useful but not landing pages, and removes five thin duplicates with no links or traffic. Queries previously split across several URLs now concentrate on the guide, and readers no longer find contradictory advice.

### Common mistakes

- Mass-deleting low-traffic pages without checking links, conversions or user value.
- Redirecting everything to the home page.
- Leaving internal links and sitemaps pointing at removed URLs.
- Pruning to "please the algorithm" instead of improving the site for readers.
keyTakeaways: Pruning means choosing keep, improve, consolidate, noindex or remove for each weak page — it is not a ranking trick.
Consolidate same-intent pages into the strongest URL with 301 redirects and updated internal links.
Redirect only to genuinely equivalent pages; home-page redirects waste value.
Use data (GSC, GA4, links) to suggest actions, and human judgement to decide.

scenes.narration: Some sites have fourteen different posts answering the same question, written over five years, each saying something slightly different. Readers get confused. Search engines see several weak pages competing with each other. In this lecture you'll learn content pruning and consolidation: the five options for every weak page, how to decide with data, how to find overlapping pages with Python, and how to merge pages without losing value.

scenes.narration: Why prune at all? Because large volumes of thin, outdated or overlapping pages confuse readers, split relevance between near duplicates, waste crawling on large sites, and, since helpful content signals became part of core ranking, can weigh on how the whole site is perceived. But here's the important part. Pruning isn't a trick. Google has said that deleting content just because it's old isn't a ranking strategy. The goal is a site where every indexable page is useful to someone.

• Confusion + cannibalisation
• Crawl waste
• Site-wide quality signals
Not a trick: aim for useful pages

scenes.narration: Here's the key idea: every weak page gets one of five decisions. Keep: it's useful to users even with low search traffic, like a refund policy or a niche answer. Improve: the topic matters but the page is weak. Consolidate: several pages cover the same intent, so merge them into the strongest URL and redirect the rest. Noindex: useful on site but not as a search landing page, like thin tag pages. And remove: no value, no links, no traffic, and nothing equivalent to redirect to.

Some duplicates get combined, you keep the best of three similar jackets. Some go in storage, still useful but not on display. And some go to charity or the bin. You don't throw out the wedding suit because you only wear it twice a year.

lessons.title: AI search, answer engines and llms.txt: what actually matters
lessons.body:
### Search is changing, not disappearing

People now get answers from **AI-powered features** inside search engines (such as Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, and Microsoft Copilot in Bing) and from **AI assistants and answer engines** such as ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude. These systems summarise information from multiple sources and sometimes cite and link to them.

This affects SEO in several ways:

- Some informational queries are answered directly, which can reduce clicks for simple facts.
- Being **cited** in AI answers can drive highly qualified visits and brand awareness.
- Content that is clear, trustworthy, well-structured and genuinely original is more likely to be used as a source.

Terms such as **GEO (generative engine optimisation)** and **AEO (answer engine optimisation)** describe this work. In practice, most of it builds on SEO fundamentals — Google's own guide to optimising for its generative AI features (May 2026) says as much, describing AEO/GEO as still SEO.

### How to be a good source for AI answers

1. **Be crawlable and indexable.** AI features in search engines generally rely on the search index. If search engines cannot crawl and index a page, it is unlikely to be used.
2. **Answer questions clearly.** Put a concise, direct answer near the top of a section, then expand. Use descriptive headings that mirror real questions.
3. **Structure content.** Lists, steps, tables, definitions and summaries are easy to extract accurately.
4. **Offer original value.** First-hand experience, original data, expert opinion and unique examples give AI systems (and people) a reason to cite you rather than a generic page.
5. **Build entity clarity.** Consistent organisation and author information, About pages, structured data (such as Organization and Person) and consistent profiles across the web help systems understand who you are.
6. **Earn mentions.** Being referenced by reputable sites, publications and communities increases the chance that AI systems encounter and trust your brand.
7. **Keep content fresh and accurate.** Outdated prices, laws or product details can be repeated in AI answers and harm trust.

### Controlling AI crawlers

Many AI companies use crawlers with published user-agent names (for example OpenAI's GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and Google-Extended, which is a control token for whether content is used for Google's Gemini models rather than a separate crawler for Search). You can allow or disallow them in robots.txt. Consider the trade-off: blocking may protect content from training use but can reduce visibility in AI answers, depending on the system. Blocking Google-Extended does not remove you from Google Search — nor from AI Overviews or AI Mode, which draw on the normal Search index. Google's controls for those are snippet directives (such as `nosnippet`, which also affects classic snippets) and, since 2026, a **Search generative AI control** in Search Console that opts a site out of AI features in Search and Discover without affecting regular results. Check each provider's current documentation, because names and behaviours change.

### What is llms.txt?

**llms.txt** is a **proposed** convention (introduced in 2024) for a Markdown file at `example.com/llms.txt` that gives language models a concise overview of a site and links to its most useful content, sometimes with a companion `llms-full.txt` containing fuller text. A simple example:

```
# Studio Noor Interiors
> Dubai interior design studio specialising in apartments and villas.

## Guides
- [Interior design cost in Dubai](https://example.com/interior-design-cost-dubai/): pricing factors and ranges
- [Small apartment ideas](https://example.com/small-apartment-ideas/)

## Company
- [About and team](https://example.com/about/)
```

Important context:

- It is **not an official web standard**. Google's May 2026 guide to generative AI features states that Google Search does not use llms.txt or other special AI files or markup: creating one neither helps nor harms visibility in Google Search, including AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- Some AI tools and developer platforms do read it, especially for documentation sites.
- It is low-cost to create and maintain, so many sites add it as an optional extra. It does **not** replace robots.txt, sitemaps, good content or technical SEO.

### Measuring AI visibility

Measurement is still maturing:

- Search Console includes clicks and impressions from Google's AI features within overall Web search performance. The **Generative AI performance report**, rolled out to all sites by the end of August 2026, adds impressions for AI Overviews, AI Mode and AI features in Discover by page, country, device and date (Google says more metrics will follow — check the current help page).
- Analytics can show referrals from AI assistants (for example, sessions from chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai) – create a channel group or segment for them.
- Manually (or with emerging tools) test important questions in AI assistants and note whether and how your brand is cited.
- Track branded search growth and direct traffic as indirect signals.

### Worked example

A UK accountancy firm finds AI assistants often answer "how to register as self-employed in the UK" without citing it. It restructures its guide with a direct summary answer, step-by-step list and links to the official GOV.UK pages, adds an author bio for a named chartered accountant, updates dates and figures, adds Organization and Person structured data and publishes an llms.txt listing its key guides. It then tracks AI referrals in analytics and checks answer citations monthly.

### What Google's May 2026 guide says to do — and to ignore

Google Search Central's guide to optimising for generative AI features is the most authoritative source for Google's AI surfaces. In summary:

| Do | You can ignore (for Google Search) |
|---|---|
| Create valuable, **non-commodity** content with a unique point of view and first-hand insight | llms.txt and other special "AI files" or markup |
| Organise content so readers can use it; add high-quality images and video | "Chunking" content into tiny fragments — Google's systems understand multi-topic pages |
| Keep pages crawlable and indexable; follow Search Essentials | Rewriting content in an "AI style" or for every long-tail variation — AI features understand synonyms |
| Use structured data as part of normal SEO (no special schema is required for AI features) | Chasing inauthentic "mentions" across the web |

It also explains **query fan-out**: for complex questions, the model issues several related searches and combines the results, so a deep page can be cited for a sub-question even if it doesn't match the exact query. And Google's spam documentation (May 2026) states that techniques aimed at manipulating generative AI responses in Search are covered by its spam policies.

Other answer engines (ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Copilot, Claude with web search) have their own crawlers and retrieval systems and publish their own documentation; some developer tools do read llms.txt. The fundamentals — crawlable, clear, original, trustworthy content and genuine mentions — transfer across all of them. For an end-to-end programme, continue with **AI Search Optimization (ai-search-optimization-geo)**.

### Hands-on: a GA4 channel for AI assistants

In GA4 (Admin → Data display → Channel groups), copy the default group and add a channel **AI assistants** above *Referral*, with *Session source* matching the regex:

```text
(^|\.)(chatgpt\.com|chat\.openai\.com|perplexity\.ai|copilot\.microsoft\.com|gemini\.google\.com|claude\.ai)$
```

Clicks from Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode still arrive as `google / organic`; use Search Console for those.

### Common mistakes

- Treating llms.txt as a ranking factor or a substitute for SEO.
- Blocking all crawlers without considering visibility trade-offs.
- Publishing generic content that offers nothing an AI summary would need to cite.
- Ignoring accuracy, which AI answers can amplify.

video.script: Search is changing. More and more people get answers from AI: Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Claude. Instead of ten blue links, they see a summary, sometimes with a few sources cited. So how do you become one of those sources? The good news is that it starts with solid SEO. If search engines can't crawl and index your page, AI features that rely on the index are unlikely to use it. Then, make your content easy to use as a source. Put a clear, direct answer near the top of each section. Use headings that match real questions. Add steps, lists and tables. Most importantly, offer something original: first-hand experience, your own data, a named expert. Generic content gives an AI system no reason to cite you. You may have heard of llms dot t x t. It's a proposed file that gives language models a short overview of your site and links to your best pages. It's cheap to create and some tools read it, but it isn't an official standard, and Google has said it isn't used for Google Search. Treat it as a small extra, never a replacement for good content. Finally, measure what you can. Track referrals from AI assistants in your analytics, test key questions regularly and watch your branded searches grow. The fundamentals haven't changed: be useful, be clear and be trustworthy.

keyTakeaways: AI Overviews, AI Mode and answer engines summarise sources; being cited requires crawlable, clear, original, trustworthy content.
Structure answers directly, build entity clarity and earn mentions from reputable sources.
AI crawlers can be managed in robots.txt; weigh visibility against content-use concerns and check current documentation.
llms.txt is an optional, proposed convention, not an official standard or ranking factor; it complements rather than replaces SEO.

lessons.title: Measuring SEO with Google Search Console
lessons.body:
### Why Search Console is essential

Google Search Console (GSC) is a free tool that shows how Google sees your site: which queries you appear for, how often people click, which pages are indexed and what technical problems exist. Bing Webmaster Tools offers similar data for Bing (which also powers some other search experiences). Set both up for every site you manage.

### Setting up

- Add a **Domain property** (verified via DNS) to cover all subdomains and protocols, or a URL-prefix property if you cannot edit DNS.
- Submit your XML sitemap.
- Give team members appropriate access (not everyone needs owner permissions).
- Link GSC with Google Analytics 4 if you want to view some Search Console data alongside analytics.

### The Performance report

Four core metrics:

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Clicks** | Times users clicked through to your site from Google Search |
| **Impressions** | Times a link to your site appeared in results a user saw (definitions vary slightly by feature) |
| **CTR** | Clicks ÷ Impressions |
| **Average position** | Average topmost position of your site in results, across impressions |

Filter by query, page, country, device, search appearance and date. Compare date ranges to spot trends (compare like-for-like periods, for example this month versus the same month last year, to account for seasonality).

### Practical analyses

**1. Quick wins: high impressions, low CTR**
Find queries or pages with many impressions and a lower CTR than similar pages. Improve titles and meta descriptions to better match intent, or improve the content so it earns richer snippets.

**2. Striking distance: positions roughly 8–20**
Pages ranking on the edge of page one can often move up with content improvements, better internal links and fresh updates.

**3. Content decay**
Compare the last three months with the previous three (or year-on-year). Pages losing clicks may need updating or may face new competition or AI features.

**4. Query-page mismatches**
If an informational blog post ranks for a transactional query, consider whether a better-matched page should exist or be linked prominently.

**5. Cannibalisation**
Filter by a query and check the Pages tab. If several of your pages swap in and out, consider consolidating.

### Indexing and experience reports

- **Page indexing report:** shows indexed and not-indexed pages with reasons (for example "Crawled – currently not indexed", "Duplicate without user-selected canonical", "Excluded by noindex tag"). Not every non-indexed URL is a problem; focus on pages you want indexed.
- **URL Inspection:** check a specific URL's index status, the canonical Google selected, and test the live URL; request indexing after important updates.
- **Core Web Vitals report:** groups of URLs with poor, needs-improvement or good performance based on real-user data.
- **Manual actions and security issues:** check regularly; hopefully always empty.
- **Links report:** top linking sites and internal link counts.

### Connecting SEO to business results

Search Console shows visibility and clicks, not revenue. Combine it with analytics and CRM data:

- In GA4, analyse organic search sessions, engagement and conversions by landing page.
- Tag conversion events (leads, purchases, bookings) and attribute them to organic landing pages.
- Report SEO as a funnel: impressions → clicks → engaged sessions → conversions → revenue.

### A monthly SEO reporting template

1. **Summary:** clicks, impressions, CTR and conversions vs previous period and last year.
2. **Top gaining and losing pages and queries** with reasons.
3. **Technical health:** indexing changes, Core Web Vitals, errors fixed.
4. **Content shipped** and early performance.
5. **Next month's priorities** (quick wins, striking-distance updates, new cluster pages).

### Worked example (illustrative)

A Lahore travel agency finds its "Hunza travel guide" page has high impressions but a low CTR, sitting around position 6. The title was "Guide | Travel Co". The team rewrites it as "Hunza Travel Guide 2026: Best Time, Routes & Costs" (reflecting content the page genuinely contains), adds an updated cost table and links from its "Northern Pakistan tours" page. Over the following weeks, CTR rises and enquiries from the page increase.

### What's new in Search Console (2025–2026)

- **Generative AI performance report** — impressions for AI Overviews, AI Mode and AI features in Discover, broken down by page, country, device and date (rolled out to all sites by the end of August 2026; additional metrics are planned). AI feature clicks and impressions also remain inside normal Web search totals.
- **Search generative AI control** — a setting that lets a site opt out of AI features in Search and Discover without affecting regular results. It's a business decision with trade-offs; read the current help page first.
- **AI-powered configuration** — Search Console added a natural-language way to set up Performance report filters and comparisons (announced December 2025); always double-check the filters it applies before drawing conclusions.

### Hands-on: a regex toolkit for the Performance report

Search Console's Query and Page filters accept **Custom (regex)** using RE2 syntax:

```text
Brand vs non-brand:     yourbrand|your brand|yb app          (then use "Doesn't match regex" for non-brand)
Questions:              ^(how|what|why|when|where|which|who|can|does|is|are)\b
Local intent:           near me|nearby|dubai|sharjah|lahore|karachi|riyadh|jeddah
Commercial:             best|top|vs|review|price|cost|cheap
Section of the site:    /blog/|/guides/          (on the Page filter)
```

Compare like-for-like periods (for example "last 3 months" vs "same period last year"), and export the result to Sheets for the analyses in this lesson. The next lesson automates this with the Search Console API.

### Common mistakes

- Judging SEO on average position alone.
- Comparing periods without considering seasonality.
- Panicking about every non-indexed URL.
- Reporting clicks without connecting them to conversions.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Search Console data with Python and Google Sheets
lessons.body:
### Why go beyond the interface

The Search Console interface shows up to 1,000 rows per table and one comparison at a time. The **Search Console API** returns far more rows, lets you combine dimensions (query × page × date), and makes monthly analyses repeatable. Data is available for roughly the last 16 months, so export regularly if you want longer history — or use Search Console's **bulk data export to BigQuery** for large sites.

### Setup (once)

1. In Google Cloud, create a project and enable the **Google Search Console API**.
2. Create a **service account** and download its JSON key. Store the key outside your code folder and point an environment variable at it.
3. In Search Console → Settings → Users and permissions, add the service account's email as a user (restricted access is enough to read data).
4. Install libraries: `pip install google-api-python-client google-auth pandas`.

### A reusable extractor with pagination

```python
import os
import time
import pandas as pd
from google.oauth2 import service_account
from googleapiclient.discovery import build
from googleapiclient.errors import HttpError

SITE = os.environ.get("GSC_SITE", "sc-domain:example.com")
creds = service_account.Credentials.from_service_account_file(
    os.environ["GSC_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON"],
    scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/webmasters.readonly"])
gsc = build("searchconsole", "v1", credentials=creds)

def fetch(start: str, end: str, dimensions: list[str], filters: list[dict] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows, start_row = [], 0
    while True:
        body = {"startDate": start, "endDate": end, "dimensions": dimensions,
                "rowLimit": 25000, "startRow": start_row}
        if filters:
            body["dimensionFilterGroups"] = [{"filters": filters}]
        for attempt in range(3):
            try:
                resp = gsc.searchanalytics().query(siteUrl=SITE, body=body).execute()
                break
            except HttpError as e:
                if attempt == 2:
                    raise
                time.sleep(2 ** attempt)          # simple backoff for quota errors
        batch = resp.get("rows", [])
        rows += [{**dict(zip(dimensions, r["keys"])), "clicks": r["clicks"],
                  "impressions": r["impressions"], "ctr": r["ctr"], "position": r["position"]}
                 for r in batch]
        if len(batch) < 25000:
            return pd.DataFrame(rows)
        start_row += 25000

if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = fetch("2026-06-01", "2026-08-31", ["query", "page"])
    df.to_csv("gsc_query_page_2026Q3.csv", index=False)
    print(len(df), "rows")
```

### Four analyses in a few lines each

```python
import re
BRAND = re.compile(r"yourbrand|your brand", re.I)
df["brand"] = df["query"].str.contains(BRAND)

# 1) Striking distance: non-brand queries ranking 8-20 with real demand
striking = df[(~df["brand"]) & df["position"].between(8, 20) & (df["impressions"] >= 200)]

# 2) Low CTR for position: compare each row with the site's median CTR at that rounded position
df["pos_bucket"] = df["position"].round().clip(1, 20)
bench = df.groupby("pos_bucket")["ctr"].median().rename("median_ctr")
df = df.join(bench, on="pos_bucket")
low_ctr = df[(df["impressions"] >= 500) & (df["ctr"] < 0.5 * df["median_ctr"])]

# 3) Cannibalisation: queries where 2+ pages each get meaningful impressions
multi = df[df["impressions"] >= 50].groupby("query")["page"].nunique()
cannibal = df[df["query"].isin(multi[multi >= 2].index)].sort_values(["query", "clicks"], ascending=[True, False])

# 4) Question queries for FAQ/cluster ideas
questions = df[df["query"].str.match(r"^(how|what|why|when|which|can|does|is|are)\b", case=False)]
```

Using your own site's median CTR by position as the benchmark avoids relying on generic industry CTR curves, which vary widely by query type and SERP features.

### Getting results into Google Sheets

The simplest route is CSV: `striking.to_csv("striking.csv", index=False)`, then **File → Import** in Sheets. For no-code users, Google Sheets add-ons and the Looker Studio Search Console connector can pull data directly; Looker Studio is a good way to share dashboards without sharing raw exports. In Sheets, useful formulas on an imported export:

```text
Brand flag:      =REGEXMATCH(LOWER(A2), "yourbrand|your brand")
CTR vs median:   =D2 / XLOOKUP(ROUND(E2), Bench!A:A, Bench!B:B)
Top pages:       =QUERY(Data!A:E, "select B, sum(C) group by B order by sum(C) desc limit 20", 1)
```

### Working responsibly with the data

- Keep the service-account key out of code and version control; restrict who can read it.
- Remember that some rare queries are anonymised: query-level totals won't match page totals.
- Annotate changes (site releases, updates, campaigns) in a shared log so trends can be interpreted.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A Karachi edtech company's content lead runs the script on the first working day of each month. Striking-distance analysis surfaces 40 non-brand queries on positions 8–20; the team refreshes six pages that cover them. The low-CTR-for-position check finds a guide whose title promises "free" courses the site no longer offers — fixing the title restores CTR. Cannibalisation output shows two near-identical posts on "freelancing skills"; they're consolidated. The monthly routine takes about two hours and replaces guesswork with a short, prioritised list.

### Common mistakes

- Pulling only 1,000 rows from the interface and assuming it's everything.
- Comparing query-level totals with page-level totals.
- Using generic CTR curves instead of your own benchmarks.
- Hard-coding credentials in scripts or notebooks.

options: It will rank first because it is long
It will rank because history pages are popular
It will struggle because it does not match the dominant intent
pool.explanation: Content must match what searchers want; the results show commercial intent.

pool.question: Select the TWO best sources of real customer language for keyword seeds.
options: Customer questions from WhatsApp and email
pool.explanation: Customer messages and reviews reveal how people actually describe problems.

pool.question: Three keywords have results pages with almost identical top-ranking URLs. How should you target them?
options: Target all three with one page, using one as primary and the others as secondary
Put each keyword in a separate domain
pool.explanation: Overlapping SERPs indicate the same intent, so one page should serve them to avoid cannibalisation.

pool.question: A client in the UAE wants to rank for both Arabic and English searches. What is the best approach?
options: Research each language separately and create properly localised pages with hreflang
Machine-translate every page and publish without review
Mix both languages randomly on each page
pool.explanation: Search behaviour differs by language; localised pages with correct hreflang serve each audience.

pool.question: How many H1 headings is it generally best practice for a page to have?
options: One clear H1 describing the topic
pool.explanation: A single clear H1 communicates the main topic.

pool.question: Which is an example of keyword stuffing?
options: Repeating 'cheap shoes Dubai' unnaturally in every sentence
Using the main keyword once in the title
pool.explanation: Unnatural repetition violates spam policies and harms readability.

pool.question: Which improvement best demonstrates first-hand experience in a hotel review?
options: Original photos and specific details from staying there
A stock image of a bed
pool.explanation: Original evidence and specifics show genuine experience.

pool.question: Select ALL elements that strengthen trust on a finance advice website.
options: Clear contact and company registration details
pool.explanation: Credentials, citations, transparency and honest dates build trust. Anonymous, undated posts undermine it.

pool.question: A site publishes 500 AI-generated city pages ('Best plumber in [town]') with identical text apart from the town name. What is the main risk?
options: It may be treated as scaled content abuse or doorway pages under spam policies
pool.explanation: Mass-produced, low-value pages created to manipulate rankings breach spam policies.

pool.question: What does YMYL mean?
options: Your Money or Your Life – topics that can significantly affect health, finances, safety or wellbeing
pool.explanation: YMYL topics face higher quality standards.

pool.question: What does an XML sitemap do?
options: Lists URLs you want search engines to discover and index
pool.explanation: Sitemaps help discovery of canonical, indexable URLs.

pool.question: What is the 'good' threshold for Largest Contentful Paint?
pool.explanation: LCP ≤ 2.5 s is good; 200 ms is the INP threshold and 0.1 the CLS threshold.

pool.question: After a redesign, organic traffic drops sharply. robots.txt contains 'Disallow: /'. What happened?
options: The staging robots.txt blocking all crawling was shipped to production
pool.explanation: A leftover staging directive blocks crawlers from the entire site.

pool.question: A product is available at several URLs with different filter parameters. What is the best way to consolidate signals?
options: Submit every variant in the sitemap
Use noindex on the preferred URL
Add canonical tags pointing to the preferred URL and link internally to it
pool.explanation: Canonicals and consistent internal links tell search engines the preferred version.

pool.question: Select the TWO correct statements about robots.txt.
options: A disallowed URL can still appear in search results if linked from elsewhere
It is the best way to remove a page from the index
It must list every page on the site
pool.explanation: robots.txt blocks crawling only; noindex (on a crawlable page) removes pages from the index.

pool.question: INP is poor on a site with chat widgets, heatmaps and several ad pixels. What is the most effective first step?
options: Audit and remove unused third-party scripts and defer the rest
pool.explanation: Heavy JavaScript on the main thread delays responses; reducing third-party scripts improves INP.

pool.question: Which structured data format does Google recommend in most cases?
pool.explanation: JSON-LD is Google's generally recommended format for structured data.

pool.question: What is a pillar page?
options: A page that lists all products
A comprehensive overview of a broad topic that links to detailed cluster pages
pool.explanation: Pillars anchor topic clusters.

pool.question: Which three factors does Google describe for local rankings?
pool.explanation: Local results weigh relevance, distance and prominence.

pool.question: A plumber without a shop serves customers at home. How should the Google Business Profile be set up?
options: Hide the address and set service areas
Create profiles for every nearby town
pool.explanation: Service-area businesses should hide their address and list the areas they serve.

pool.question: Select the TWO practices that break review rules or law in many markets.
options: Writing reviews of your own business under fake names
Sending a review link to customers after a purchase
pool.explanation: Fake or self-written reviews breach platform policies and consumer protection laws. Responding and asking genuine customers are good practice.

pool.question: A franchise creates 40 location pages with identical text except the city name. Rankings are poor. What is the best fix?
options: Add more city names to each page
Give each page unique, useful local content such as team, directions, photos and local reviews
pool.explanation: Near-duplicate doorway pages add little value; unique local information helps users and rankings.

pool.question: Your cluster's pages are ranking, but the pillar receives few internal links and little traffic. What should you do?
options: Add contextual links from every cluster page to the pillar and improve the pillar's substance
Add links only from the footer
pool.explanation: Strong two-way internal linking and a genuinely useful pillar are central to the model.

pool.question: In Search Console, how is CTR calculated?
pool.explanation: CTR is clicks divided by impressions.

pool.question: Which statement about llms.txt is accurate?
options: It is an official web standard required for ranking
It is an optional proposed convention and not a substitute for SEO
pool.explanation: llms.txt is a proposed convention, not an official standard. Google's May 2026 guide says Google Search doesn't use it, so it neither helps nor harms Google visibility; some other tools may read it. It never substitutes for SEO fundamentals.

pool.question: Which pages are good 'striking distance' opportunities?
options: Pages averaging roughly positions 8–20 for valuable queries
pool.explanation: Pages near the top of page one or on page two can often move up with targeted improvements.

pool.question: Select ALL tactics that make content more likely to be cited in AI answers.
options: Concise direct answers under question-style headings
Hiding main content behind scripts crawlers cannot render
pool.explanation: Clear answers under descriptive headings, original data or first-hand experience, and clear author and organisation information all make content more useful and citable. Note that Google's May 2026 guidance says you don't need to 'chunk' content or create special AI files — these tactics work because they are good content practice, not AI tricks.

pool.question: Clicks fell 30% year-on-year for an informational guide while impressions stayed flat and average position is unchanged. What is a plausible explanation to investigate?
options: More answers are being satisfied on the results page (for example by AI features), reducing CTR
pool.explanation: Flat impressions and position with fewer clicks point to lower CTR, which AI summaries and SERP features can cause.

pool.question: A manager wants SEO success measured only by average position. What is the best argument for a broader view?
options: Average position hides query mix and does not show clicks, conversions or revenue
Search Console does not show position
pool.explanation: SEO should be reported as a funnel from impressions to revenue; position alone is misleading.

pool.question: Which Search Console tool lets you check the canonical Google selected for a specific page?
pool.explanation: URL Inspection shows index status and the Google-selected canonical.

pool.question: A news site offers a partner a revenue share to publish 'best casino bonuses' pages under its domain, written and managed by the partner. Which policy applies?
options: Site reputation abuse — first-party involvement doesn't make it acceptable
pool.explanation: Third-party content hosted mainly to exploit the host's ranking signals is site reputation abuse; Google clarified in November 2024 that first-party oversight doesn't change that.

pool.question: Which TWO statements about AI-generated content reflect Google's guidance?
options: Using AI to help create content isn't against Google's guidelines
Generating many pages primarily to manipulate rankings is scaled content abuse however they're produced
Labelling AI content guarantees it ranks
pool.explanation: Google judges purpose and quality; scaled content abuse applies regardless of production method.

pool.question: What does Google mean by 'non-commodity' content in its May 2026 guidance?
options: Content offering unique insight or first-hand perspective beyond common knowledge
pool.explanation: Google contrasts generic tips with first-hand, specific content; the latter is more useful in both classic results and AI answers.

pool.question: A publisher blocks Google-Extended in robots.txt expecting to disappear from AI Overviews. What actually happens?
options: Pages disappear from Google Search entirely
It affects use for Gemini training/grounding, not AI Overviews or AI Mode, which use the normal Search index
Nothing; Google-Extended is not a real token
pool.explanation: Google-Extended controls Gemini training and some grounding uses. AI Overviews/AI Mode are governed by Search controls such as snippet directives and Search Console's generative AI control.

pool.question: The CrUX API returns 'not found' for a small page. What's the best next step?
options: Query the origin-level data or use lab tests, because the page lacks enough real-user data
pool.explanation: CrUX only has URL-level data for pages with enough traffic; use origin data or lab tools instead.

pool.question: Which internal linking practice best supports topical authority?
options: Contextual body links with descriptive, varied anchors from strong pages to related pages that need help
Linking only from the home page
pool.explanation: Contextual, descriptive links help readers and search engines understand relationships and distribute signals.

pool.question: Which review practice breaks Google Business Profile policies?
options: Sending every customer the same neutral review link
Asking customers to mention a staff member by name in their review
Using a QR code on receipts
pool.explanation: Google prohibits soliciting reviews with specific content, including content identifying staff members.

pool.question: A brief lists the keyword and word count but no angle or expert. What is the main risk when an AI tool drafts from it?
options: The page will be too short
A fluent but generic, commodity page with nothing others lack
pool.explanation: With cheap drafting, the brief's non-commodity angle and expert input decide quality.

pool.question: Which TWO controls best keep an AI-assisted workflow honest?
options: Drafting only from the brief and expert notes, with [MISSING] and [VERIFY] markers instead of invented facts
An expert sign-off and source check before publishing (especially YMYL)
Publishing whatever the model returns to save time
Asking the AI to fact-check itself as the only review
pool.explanation: Markers make gaps visible and human expert review provides accountability; self-review by the model is not fact-checking.

pool.question: Editors are approving 80 AI drafts a week at two minutes each. What should the content lead do?
options: Reduce volume to match genuine editorial and expert review capacity
pool.explanation: When review becomes a rubber stamp, the programme risks low-value scaled content.

pool.question: A page's impressions are flat, position unchanged, and clicks down 30% year-on-year. What's the most likely cause?
options: SERP changes (for example AI Overviews or other features) reducing CTR
pool.explanation: Stable impressions and position with falling clicks point to SERP changes; refresh around what still earns a click.

pool.question: When should you update a page's visible 'last updated' date?
options: Only after a material content change
pool.explanation: Changing dates without substantial changes misleads readers; Google advises against it.

pool.question: Five old posts target the same intent; one has most links and traffic. What's the best consolidation approach?
options: Merge unique content into the strongest URL, 301 the others to it, update internal links and the sitemap
Redirect all to the home page
pool.explanation: Consolidating into the strongest URL preserves value; home-page redirects act like soft 404s.

pool.question: What does Search Console's Generative AI performance report add (as rolled out in 2026)?
options: Impressions for AI Overviews, AI Mode and AI features in Discover by page, country, device and date
A list of every AI prompt users typed
pool.explanation: The report shows AI feature impressions with breakdowns; Google has said more metrics will follow.

pool.question: Your API analysis flags a query at position 3 with CTR far below generic industry curves. Why check your own median CTR by position first?
options: CTR varies with SERP features (AI Overviews, ads, carousels); your own benchmark reflects your real SERPs
pool.explanation: Benchmarks from your own data are more reliable than generic curves that ignore SERP layout differences.

pool.question: Where do clicks from Google's AI Overviews appear in GA4 by default?
pool.explanation: They arrive as normal Google organic traffic; use Search Console's reports for AI feature impressions.
